title: Grandma's birthday
text: My name is Ben and I am twelve years old. I live in Cork, in Ireland, with my family. My mum is a nurse. She works at night and sleeps in the morning. My dad drives a bus. He is tall and he laughs a lot. I have two sisters. Kate is sixteen and she plays the guitar in her room. Lucy is only four and she asks questions all day. We have an old dog too. His name is Max. Every Sunday we have lunch at my grandmother's house. Grandma always cooks chicken and potatoes for everyone. But today is different. It is Grandma's birthday, so we cook for her. Dad makes soup and Kate makes a big chocolate cake. Grandma sits in her chair and smiles. She says it is her best birthday.

gloss.nurse: a person who helps sick people
gloss.night: the dark time, when people sleep
gloss.drives: makes a bus or car go (drive)
gloss.sisters: girls with the same parents as you (sister)
gloss.guitar: a thing with strings for making music
gloss.questions: things you say when you want to know something
gloss.lunch: the meal in the middle of the day
gloss.grandmother: the mother of your mother or father
gloss.chicken: a farm bird, or its meat
gloss.potatoes: white vegetables from under the ground (potato)
gloss.birthday: the day you were born, each year
gloss.soup: hot food that you eat with a spoon
gloss.cake: a soft, sweet food, often for a birthday

questions.q: What job does Ben's mother do?
What does Kate play in her room?
What does Kate make for Grandma?

notice: In the present, add -s to the verb after he, she, it or a name: "She works at night", "he laughs a lot". After I, we and they there is no -s.

title: Late for the ferry
text: My name is Mia. I live in Sydney and I work in an office in the city. Every morning I get up at six o'clock. I have a shower and get dressed. Then I make breakfast. I eat toast with butter and I drink a cup of tea. At seven I walk to the ferry. The boat trip takes twenty minutes and I love it. I sit outside and look at the water. But this morning is different. I open my eyes and it is eight o'clock. I am very late! I do not eat. I take my bag and run to the ferry. Then I stop. There are no people in suits, only families with children. I look at my phone. It is Saturday! I laugh, buy a coffee and sit in the sun.

gloss.office: a place where people work at desks
gloss.o'clock: a word used with the hour: six o'clock
gloss.breakfast: the first meal of the day
gloss.butter: soft yellow food made from milk
gloss.cup: a small thing you drink from
gloss.tea: a hot drink made from leaves
gloss.ferry: a boat that takes people across water
gloss.boat: a thing that carries people on water
gloss.trip: going from one place to another
gloss.bag: a thing you carry your things in
gloss.suits: jackets and trousers for office work (suit)
gloss.sun: the big light in the sky in the day

questions.q: What does Mia drink at breakfast?
How does Mia go to work?
What day of the week is it in the story?

notice: For things you do again and again, use the present simple, often with every: "Every morning I get up at six o'clock". The negative uses do not: "I do not eat".

title: At the café
text: It is a cold Monday in London. At one o'clock, Emma goes into a small café near her office. She is hungry and a little tired. "Hello," says the waiter. "What would you like?" "A cup of tea and a cheese sandwich, please," says Emma. She sits at a table by the window. Outside, it is raining and people are walking fast. The waiter brings her tea and her sandwich. They are very good. Then Emma opens her bag. Oh no! Her wallet is not there. It is at home, on the kitchen table. Her face goes red. She tells the waiter. He smiles. "No problem," he says. "You can pay tomorrow." The next day, Emma comes back. She pays for her lunch and gives the waiter a small box of chocolates.

gloss.o'clock: a word used with the hour: one o'clock
gloss.goes: goes into: walks in; goes red: turns red
gloss.café: a place that sells drinks and small meals
gloss.office: a place where people work at desks
gloss.waiter: a man who brings food to your table
gloss.would: would like: want (a polite way to say it)
gloss.cup: a small thing you drink from
gloss.cheese: a yellow or white food made from milk
gloss.sandwich: two pieces of bread with food between them
gloss.window: the glass part of a wall
gloss.raining: water is falling from the sky (rain)
gloss.bag: a thing you carry your things in
gloss.wallet: a small flat case for money and cards
gloss.problem: no problem: it is all right
gloss.next: the next day: the day after
gloss.lunch: the meal in the middle of the day
gloss.box: a thing with flat sides for keeping things in
gloss.chocolates: small sweet brown things to eat

questions.q: What does Emma order to drink?
Where is Emma's wallet?
What does Emma give the waiter the next day?

notice: To order, name the thing and add please: "A cup of tea and a cheese sandwich, please". Staff often ask with would like, a polite form of want: "What would you like?"

title: The Saturday market
text: Last Saturday, Maria went to the farmers' market near her apartment in Seattle. Sunday was her son's birthday, and she wanted to make him a strawberry cake. The market was busy and noisy, and the air smelled of fresh bread. A man was playing the guitar near the entrance. First she bought eggs, tomatoes and a jar of honey. Then she looked for strawberries, but every stand was sold out. Maria was worried. At the last stand, an old farmer saw her sad face. "No strawberries today," he said, "but my peaches are the sweetest in the city. Try one." Maria tasted a piece. It was delicious. She bought a big bag of peaches and carried it home. That evening she made a peach cake instead. The next day, her son ate three pieces. "Mom," he said, "can we have this cake every year?"

gloss.farmers: people who grow food to sell (farmer)
gloss.market: a place outside where people sell food and other things
gloss.apartment: a home on one floor of a building
gloss.air: what you breathe; it is all around you
gloss.smelled: had a smell (smell); you smell with your nose
gloss.guitar: a thing with strings for making music
gloss.honey: sweet, thick food made by bees
gloss.stand: a table where someone sells things at a market
gloss.sold: sold out: with nothing left to buy (sell)
gloss.worried: afraid that something would go wrong
gloss.farmer: a person who grows food on a farm
gloss.peaches: soft, round, sweet fruits with yellow and red skin (peach)
gloss.peach: a soft, round, sweet fruit with yellow and red skin
gloss.sweetest: the most sweet, with the most taste of sugar
gloss.tasted: ate a little to see if it was good (taste)
gloss.instead: in place of the other thing

questions.q: What kind of cake did Maria want to make at first?
Who gave Maria a piece of fruit to taste?
Which fruit did Maria use for the cake in the end?

notice: Many common verbs have an irregular past form, which you learn one by one: "she bought eggs" (buy), "her son ate three pieces" (eat).

title: A weekend at the beach
text: Last weekend, my sister and I drove from Auckland to a small beach town in the north. We left early on Saturday, but the roads were busy and the trip took five hours. When we arrived, it was raining hard. The sea was grey and the beach was empty. We sat in a little café, ate fish and chips and watched the rain through the window. My sister wanted to drive home. "Let's wait until tomorrow," I said. On Sunday morning, the sky was blue and the sun was shining. We ran down to the beach before breakfast. The water was cold, but we swam anyway. Suddenly my sister shouted and pointed at the sea. Three dolphins were jumping in the waves, not far from us. We watched them until they disappeared. On the way home, we were tired and hungry, but we couldn't stop smiling. Next time, we will stay for a whole week.

gloss.north: the top part of a country on a map
gloss.early: near the start of the day
gloss.trip: the drive from one place to another
gloss.grey: the colour between black and white
gloss.café: a place that sells drinks and simple meals
gloss.through: from one side to the other
gloss.dolphins: clever sea animals that jump out of the water (dolphin)
gloss.waves: water that rises and falls on the sea (wave)
gloss.disappeared: went where we could not see them (disappear)

questions.q: What was the weather like when they arrived?
What did they eat in the café?
Which animals did they see in the waves?

notice: Was or were + -ing shows something in progress at a moment in the past: "it was raining hard", "Three dolphins were jumping in the waves".

title: The new flat
text: Last month, Priya moved to a new flat in Manchester. Her old flat was cheap, but it was dark and far from her office. The new one is on the top floor of an old building, and there is no lift. On moving day, two friends came to help her with a van. The van was too small for all her things, so they had to make three trips. They carried heavy boxes up the stairs all afternoon. By the evening, everybody was exhausted and the flat was full of boxes. Priya wanted to make tea, but she couldn't find the box with the kettle. Then somebody knocked on the door. It was an old woman from the flat downstairs. Priya was afraid that she was angry about the noise. But her new neighbour was carrying a tray with a pot of tea and a plate of biscuits. "Welcome to the building," she said. Priya smiled. She already felt at home.

gloss.moved: went to live in a new place (move)
gloss.flat: a home on one floor of a building
gloss.lift: a machine that carries people up and down
gloss.moving: moving day: the day you change homes
gloss.van: a big car for carrying things
gloss.kettle: a pot for making water hot for tea
gloss.knocked: hit the door to say I am here (knock)
gloss.neighbour: a person who lives near you
gloss.tray: a flat thing for carrying food and drinks
gloss.pot: a round container; this one is for tea
gloss.biscuits: small, dry, sweet things to eat with tea (biscuit)
gloss.welcome: we are happy that you are here
gloss.felt: felt at home: was happy and relaxed there (feel)

questions.q: What was wrong with Priya's old flat?
What could Priya not find in the evening?
What did the neighbour bring on a tray?

notice: Had to and couldn't are the past forms of must and can't: "they had to make three trips", "she couldn't find the box".

title: A visit to the doctor
text: For two weeks, Daniel had a headache every evening. He slept badly and he felt tired at work. On Monday he finally went to see a doctor near his apartment in Toronto. He waited for almost an hour in the waiting room. Then the doctor called his name. She asked him a lot of questions. Did he drink enough water? Did he sleep well? How many hours did he spend at his computer? "About ten hours a day," said Daniel. The doctor checked his eyes and asked him to read some small letters on the wall. He couldn't read the last three lines. "You don't need medicine," she said. "You need glasses." A week later, Daniel got his first pair of glasses, and his headaches stopped. Now he can see everything clearly. Unfortunately, he can also see how dirty his windows are.

gloss.apartment: a home on one floor of a building
gloss.waited: stayed there until his turn came (wait)
gloss.waiting: waiting room: where you sit before you see the doctor
gloss.letters: the signs we write words with, like A and B
gloss.wall: one of the sides of a room
gloss.medicine: something you take to get better when you are ill
gloss.glasses: two pieces of glass that you wear to see better
gloss.clearly: in a way that is easy to see

questions.q: What problem did Daniel have every evening?
What did the doctor say Daniel needed?
What is dirty in Daniel's home?

notice: Questions in the past use did + the base form of the verb: "Did he sleep well?", "How many hours did he spend at his computer?"

title: The lost phone
text: Yesterday evening, Kate took the bus home from work in Edinburgh. She was tired, so she listened to music on her phone and closed her eyes. When she got home, she put her hand in her coat pocket. The phone wasn't there. She looked in her bag and then in every pocket again. Nothing. All her photos, her tickets and her friends' numbers were on that phone. She ran next door and asked her neighbour for help. He called her number. It rang for a long time, and then a man answered. It was the bus driver. "I found it under a seat," he said. "I finish work at nine. You can collect it from the bus station." Kate thanked him at least five times. When she got the phone back, there was a new photo on it. In the picture, the driver was smiling and holding a note. The note said, "Please don't lose me again."

gloss.got: got home: arrived home; got it back: had it again (get)
gloss.coat: a warm thing you wear over your clothes outside
gloss.pocket: a small bag in your clothes for keys or money
gloss.tickets: things that show you have paid (ticket)
gloss.door: next door: in the home beside hers
gloss.neighbour: a person who lives near you
gloss.rang: made the sound of a phone (ring)
gloss.answered: picked up the phone and spoke (answer)
gloss.driver: the person who drives the bus
gloss.found: saw a thing that was lost (find)
gloss.station: the place where buses start and stop
gloss.note: a few words on a piece of paper
gloss.lose: not know where a thing is any more

questions.q: How did Kate travel home from work?
Who found Kate's phone?
What was new on the phone when Kate got it back?

notice: When joins two past actions. If the when part comes first, put a comma after it: "When she got home, she put her hand in her coat pocket", "When she got the phone back, there was a new photo on it".

title: The delayed train
text: I had prepared for the interview for weeks, so I caught an early train from Bristol to London, just to be safe. For the first hour everything went well. Then, somewhere in the countryside, the train slowed down and stopped. After ten minutes, the driver announced that a tree had fallen on the line. We would be delayed for at least an hour. I looked at my watch and felt sick. My interview was at eleven, and now I was never going to make it. I decided to phone the company and explain. While I was waiting for someone to answer, a phone started ringing a few seats behind me. "Hello, Sandra speaking," said a voice in the carriage and in my ear at the same time. I stood up slowly and turned around. The woman who was supposed to interview me was sitting three rows away. We both burst out laughing. She invited me to sit down, and we did the interview right there. A week later, I got the job.

gloss.interview: a meeting to choose a person for a job
gloss.caught: got on a train or bus (catch)
gloss.safe: just to be safe: so that nothing could go wrong
gloss.countryside: land with fields and farms, outside towns
gloss.slowed: slowed down: went less and less fast (slow down)
gloss.line: the metal track that trains run on
gloss.watch: a small clock worn on the arm
gloss.sick: felt sick: felt ill in my stomach
gloss.company: a business that people work for
gloss.ringing: making the sound of a phone (ring)
gloss.voice: the sound a person makes when speaking
gloss.carriage: one of the long parts of a train, with seats
gloss.stood: stood up: got up on my feet (stand)
gloss.turned: turned around: moved to look behind me (turn)
gloss.supposed: was supposed to: had the job or plan to
gloss.burst: burst out laughing: suddenly started to laugh
gloss.right: right there: in that same place

questions.q: Which city was the writer travelling to?
What had fallen on the line?
Where did the interview take place in the end?

notice: Was going to and was supposed to describe a plan or an expectation in the past: "now I was never going to make it", "The woman who was supposed to interview me".

title: A birthday surprise
text: My father always says he doesn't want anything for his birthday. This year he was turning seventy, so my sister and I decided to ignore him. We told him that we were taking him out for a quiet dinner at his favorite restaurant in Boston. What he didn't know was that we had been planning something bigger for months. Dad grew up in Ireland, and he hadn't seen his best friend from school, Tom, for almost forty years. They had lost touch when Dad moved to America. My sister found Tom online, and he agreed to fly over. At the restaurant, Dad complained that we were making too much fuss. Then the door opened and an old man with white hair walked in. Dad stared at him for a few seconds without saying a word. "You're late," he said at last, "by about forty years." Then they hugged each other, and everyone at the table cried. Dad still says he doesn't want presents. But he calls Tom every Sunday.

gloss.turning: turning seventy: becoming seventy years old
gloss.favorite: liked more than all the others
gloss.grew: grew up: was a child and became an adult (grow up)
gloss.lost: lost touch: stopped writing and talking to each other (lose)
gloss.touch: lost touch: stopped writing and talking to each other
gloss.complained: said he was not happy about something (complain)
gloss.stared: looked for a long time without moving his eyes (stare)
gloss.seconds: very short moments; sixty make a minute (second)
gloss.last: at last: in the end, after a wait
gloss.hugged: put their arms around each other (hug)
gloss.presents: things you give someone on a birthday (present)

questions.q: Where did they tell their father they were taking him?
In which country did the father grow up?
What does the father do every Sunday now?

notice: The past perfect (had + past participle) is for something that happened before another moment in the past: "he hadn't seen his best friend from school", "They had lost touch when Dad moved to America".

title: A cooking disaster
text: When I moved to Dublin, my new neighbours invited me to dinner. I was so grateful that I promised to cook for them the following week. This was a mistake, because I can barely boil an egg. I chose a recipe for roast chicken with lemon that looked simple enough in the video. On Saturday afternoon, everything went wrong. I forgot to turn the oven on for the first forty minutes. Then, to save time, I turned it up as high as it would go. While I was setting the table, the smoke alarm went off. The chicken was black on the outside and still raw in the middle. Worse, I had used salt instead of sugar in the chocolate cake. My guests arrived to find every window open and me almost in tears. Fortunately, they thought it was hilarious. We ordered pizza and ate it on the balcony, and they stayed until midnight. Since then, we have had dinner together every month. They do the cooking, and I bring the dessert from the bakery.

gloss.promised: said I would surely do it (promise)
gloss.enough: simple enough: as simple as I needed
gloss.went: went wrong: was a failure; went off: started to ring (go)
gloss.oven: the hot box in a kitchen for baking
gloss.turned: turned it up: made it hotter (turn up)
gloss.setting: setting the table: putting out plates, knives and forks
gloss.smoke: the grey cloud that rises from a fire
gloss.alarm: a machine that rings loudly when there is danger
gloss.salt: white powder from the sea that gives food more taste
gloss.guests: people you invite to your home (guest)
gloss.ordered: asked a restaurant to send food (order)
gloss.balcony: a small outside floor on the side of a building
gloss.dessert: the sweet dish at the end of a meal
gloss.bakery: a shop that sells bread and cakes

questions.q: Who did the writer promise to cook for?
What did the writer put in the cake instead of sugar?
What did they eat in the end?

notice: Phrasal verbs join a verb and a short word to make a new meaning: "the smoke alarm went off" (began to ring), "I turned it up" (made it hotter).

title: My first day
text: On my first day at a new company in Vancouver, I arrived twenty minutes early, wearing my best jacket. The receptionist gave me a visitor's badge and told me that my manager was stuck in traffic. "There's a team meeting in room four," she said. "Why don't you join them?" I found the room, sat down at the back and tried to look confident. For an hour, people discussed an advertising campaign for a new kind of dog food. I was surprised, because I had been hired as an accountant, but I took careful notes anyway. Near the end, someone asked if the new person had any ideas. Everybody turned to look at me. I said the first thing that came into my head, something about happy dogs, and to my relief, they liked it. Then my real manager appeared at the door, out of breath. I had been sitting in the wrong meeting. The right one was in room four on the floor above. My colleagues still tease me about it. But last month, I saw my idea on a poster at a bus stop.

gloss.receptionist: the person at the front desk who welcomes visitors
gloss.visitor: a person who comes for a short time
gloss.badge: a small card with a name, worn on your clothes
gloss.manager: the person who leads a team at work
gloss.traffic: all the cars on the road
gloss.team: a group of people who work together
gloss.meeting: a time when people sit together to talk about work
gloss.advertising: telling people about a product so that they buy it
gloss.campaign: a plan of many advertisements for one product
gloss.surprised: feeling that this was not what I expected
gloss.accountant: a person who looks after a company's money
gloss.careful: done with a lot of attention
gloss.notes: short things you write down to remember (note)
gloss.relief: to my relief: I was glad, because I had been worried
gloss.appeared: came where I could see them (appear)
gloss.breath: out of breath: breathing fast after running
gloss.tease: laugh at in a friendly way
gloss.poster: a big printed picture or notice on a wall

questions.q: Why was the manager late?
What kind of food was the advertising campaign for?
Where did the writer later see the idea?

notice: In reported speech the verb moves back into the past, and a yes or no question is reported with if: "told me that my manager was stuck in traffic", "someone asked if the new person had any ideas".

title: Learning to swim
text: Grace grew up in a small town in the middle of Australia, hundreds of kilometres from the sea. Nobody had ever taught her to swim, and for years it didn't matter. Then she moved to Perth, where people seem to spend half their lives in the water. At the beach, she was always the one who stayed on the sand and looked after everybody's towels. When she turned forty-five, her friends started planning a trip to a famous reef. Grace decided that she had done enough watching. She signed up for an adult beginners' class at the local pool. The first lessons were embarrassing. Children in the next lane were swimming like fish while she held on to the wall. "Stop fighting the water," her teacher kept saying. "Let it carry you." Slowly, she learned to float, then to breathe, then to swim a whole length without stopping. Six months later, she was floating above the reef with her friends when a turtle swam past. These days, somebody else has to look after the towels.

gloss.grew: grew up: was a child and became an adult (grow up)
gloss.middle: the centre, far from the edges
gloss.hundreds: hundreds of: a very large number of
gloss.kilometres: a kilometre is a thousand metres
gloss.sand: the soft yellow ground on a beach
gloss.turned: turned forty-five: became forty-five years old
gloss.reef: a line of rock or coral just under the sea
gloss.enough: as much as she wanted, no more
gloss.signed: signed up: put her name down to join (sign up)
gloss.adult: a grown person, not a child
gloss.beginners: people who are starting to learn something (beginner)
gloss.embarrassing: making you feel shy and a little silly
gloss.lane: one of the long narrow parts of a swimming pool
gloss.held: held on to: kept her hands on (hold)
gloss.fighting: pushing against, as if it were an enemy (fight)
gloss.kept: kept saying: said again and again (keep)
gloss.float: stay on top of the water
gloss.breathe: take air in and let it out
gloss.length: the way from one end of the pool to the other
gloss.floating: lying on top of the water (float)
gloss.turtle: a sea animal with a hard round shell
gloss.swam: swam past: went by her in the water (swim)

questions.q: At the beach, what did Grace always look after?
What did the teacher tell Grace to stop fighting?
Which animal swam past Grace at the reef?

notice: Who and where can begin a clause that says more about a person or a place: "the one who stayed on the sand", "Perth, where people seem to spend half their lives in the water".

title: The letter in the attic
text: When Hannah bought an old wooden house in Nova Scotia, the attic was the last room she got around to clearing. It was crammed with broken chairs, rusty tools and boxes that had not been opened for decades. One rainy afternoon, while she was sweeping the floor, she noticed that one of the boards was loose. Underneath it lay a small tin box, and inside the box was an envelope marked "To whoever lives here next." The letter had been written more than sixty years earlier by a boy called Peter, who was eleven at the time. His family was about to move away, he explained. He was worried about the apple tree he had planted behind the house. Would the new owner please water it in dry summers? Hannah looked out of the window. The tree was still there, taller than the roof and covered in blossom. Curious, she asked around the town until somebody remembered the family's name. It took her several weeks to track Peter down. He turned out to be a retired teacher in his seventies, living in Halifax. That September, he drove out to visit, and they picked the apples together. He admitted that he had never expected anyone to read his letter, let alone to answer it.

gloss.attic: the room under the roof of a house
gloss.got: got around to: finally found time for
gloss.crammed: very full, with things pushed in
gloss.rusty: covered with the red-brown stuff that forms on old metal
gloss.tools: things you hold to do a job, like a hammer (tool)
gloss.sweeping: cleaning the floor with a brush (sweep)
gloss.boards: long flat pieces of wood in a floor (board)
gloss.envelope: the paper cover of a letter
gloss.marked: with these words written on it
gloss.whoever: the person who, any person who
gloss.about: was about to: was going to, very soon
gloss.worried: afraid that something bad would happen
gloss.planted: put into the ground to grow (plant)
gloss.roof: the top cover of a house
gloss.blossom: the flowers of a fruit tree in spring
gloss.several: more than two, but not many
gloss.track: track down: find after a long search
gloss.turned: turned out to be: was, as she found in the end
gloss.retired: no longer working because of age
gloss.seventies: in his seventies: between seventy and seventy-nine years old
gloss.admitted: said something he was a little shy about (admit)

questions.q: Where was the tin box hidden?
What had Peter planted behind the house?
What job had Peter done before he retired?

notice: The past perfect passive (had been + past participle) tells what was done to something earlier, without saying who did it: "boxes that had not been opened for decades", "The letter had been written more than sixty years earlier".

title: The bookshop on the high street
text: For as long as I can remember, there has been a bookshop on the high street of our Yorkshire town. Its owner, Margaret, has run it for thirty years and seems to have read every book on her shelves. Last month, a notice appeared in the window. The rent was going up again, it said, and unless something changed, the shop would close in the spring. The news spread quickly. People who had not set foot in the place for years declared that the town would not be the same without it. I was as upset as anyone. Then I realised, with some embarrassment, that I had not bought a book there for over a year. Like most of my neighbours, I had got into the habit of shopping online. On the internet, books were cheaper, and I did not have to leave the sofa. If the shop was in trouble, it was partly my fault. So a few of us decided to do more than complain. We started a monthly book club and persuaded the local school to order its books from Margaret. We also promised to buy all our presents from her. Whether that will be enough, nobody knows. But the shop was crowded last Saturday, and Margaret was far too busy to look worried.

gloss.high: high street: the main shopping street of a British town
gloss.owner: the person a shop belongs to
gloss.seems: seems to have: looks as if she has
gloss.shelves: long flat boards where books stand (shelf)
gloss.notice: a sheet of paper with news for people to read
gloss.rent: money paid every month to use a building
gloss.declared: said firmly, for all to hear (declare)
gloss.embarrassment: the feeling of being ashamed in front of others
gloss.habit: something you do often, without thinking
gloss.partly: in some way, but not completely
gloss.fault: my fault: something I am to blame for
gloss.complain: say that you are not happy about something
gloss.club: a group that meets to do something together
gloss.persuaded: made someone agree by giving good reasons (persuade)
gloss.promised: said we would surely do it (promise)
gloss.presents: gifts, for a birthday for example (present)
gloss.worried: afraid that something bad will happen

questions.q: What appeared in the shop window last month?
Where had the writer been buying things for the past year?
What did the group of neighbours start?

notice: In reported speech, will becomes would: "the shop would close in the spring", "the town would not be the same without it".

title: The community garden
text: Three years ago, the lot behind our apartment building in Philadelphia was nothing but weeds and broken glass. Today it is a community garden with twenty raised beds, a row of fruit trees and a waiting list. I joined mainly to get out of the house, having never grown anything more demanding than a houseplant. Last summer, however, the garden nearly fell apart. Vegetables began disappearing overnight, first a few tomatoes, then entire rows of beans. Tempers rose at our monthly meeting. Some members demanded a tall fence with a lock. Others argued that a locked garden would no longer belong to the neighborhood. In the end, we agreed to find out who was responsible before deciding anything. Two of us kept watch one evening, expecting teenagers. Instead, we saw an elderly man from across the street, filling a small bag with great care. He had lost his job the year before, it turned out, and had been too proud to ask for help. Nobody mentioned a fence again. We built a table by the gate, where gardeners now leave whatever they can spare, under a sign that says "Help yourself." The man comes every Tuesday. These days he brings his own gloves and does most of the weeding.

gloss.lot: a piece of land in a city
gloss.weeds: wild plants that grow where nobody wants them (weed)
gloss.community: the people who live in one area
gloss.raised: raised beds: boxes of earth for growing plants
gloss.beds: raised beds: boxes of earth for growing plants
gloss.row: a line of things side by side
gloss.waiting: waiting list: the names of people who want a place
gloss.grown: made a plant live and get bigger (grow)
gloss.demanding: needing a lot of work or care
gloss.houseplant: a plant kept in a pot indoors
gloss.fell: fell apart: broke up, stopped working as a group (fall)
gloss.apart: fell apart: broke up, stopped working as a group
gloss.beans: long thin green vegetables, or their seeds (bean)
gloss.fence: a wall of wood or wire around a piece of land
gloss.lock: a metal thing that keeps a gate shut
gloss.neighborhood: the streets around your home and the people in them
gloss.kept: kept watch: stayed and looked carefully (keep)
gloss.teenagers: young people from thirteen to nineteen (teenager)
gloss.turned: it turned out: we learned later
gloss.proud: not wanting to show that you need help
gloss.spare: give away because they have more than they need

questions.q: What was the lot full of three years ago?
What did some members want to put around the garden?
What did the gardeners build by the gate?

notice: An -ing clause after a comma adds what someone was doing or thinking, with no new sentence: "Two of us kept watch one evening, expecting teenagers", "filling a small bag with great care".

title: At the bakery
lines: Good morning! What can I get you?
Good morning. Can I have a loaf of brown bread, please?
I'm sorry, the brown bread is all gone. We have white bread and fresh rolls.
That's okay. I'll take four rolls, please.
Here you are. Would you like anything else?
Yes, please. How much are the apple cakes?
They're two pounds each.
Good. I'd like two apple cakes, please.
Of course. That's six pounds, please.
Can I pay by card?
Yes, no problem. Put your card here, please.
Thank you very much. Have a nice day!
Thanks, you too. Goodbye!

gloss.get: what can I get you: what do you want
gloss.brown: dark, like the colour of chocolate
gloss.sorry: a polite word you say before bad news
gloss.gone: all gone: there is no more
gloss.rolls: small round breads for one person (roll)
gloss.much: how much: what is the price
gloss.card: a small bank card that you pay with

questions.q: Which bread is all gone?
How does the customer pay?

notice: Can I ...? is an easy, polite way to ask for something: "Can I have a loaf of brown bread, please?", "Can I pay by card?"

title: Asking the way
lines: Excuse me. Can you help me, please?
Sure. What are you looking for?
I'm looking for the art museum. Is it near here?
Yes, it's not far. It's about ten minutes on foot.
Good. How do I get there?
Go straight for two blocks. Then turn left at the bank.
Sorry, can you say that again more slowly?
Of course. Go straight. At the bank, turn left. The museum is next to the park.
Straight, then left at the bank. Is the museum open today?
Oh, wait. Today is Monday. The art museum is closed on Mondays.
Oh no! Is there another museum near here?
Yes, the history museum is open every day. It's across the street from the art museum.
Great. Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome. Have a good day!

gloss.excuse: excuse me: polite words for starting to talk to someone
gloss.art: paintings and other beautiful things that people make
gloss.museum: a building where you can see art or old things
gloss.blocks: the parts of a street between two corners (block)
gloss.turn: change the way you are going
gloss.bank: a place that keeps people's money
gloss.next: next to: at the side of
gloss.park: a green place in a city, with trees and grass
gloss.across: across the street from: on the other side of the street
gloss.welcome: you're welcome: a polite answer to thank you

questions.q: Where does the visitor turn left?
On which day is the art museum closed?

notice: To tell someone the way, use the verb with no subject: "Go straight for two blocks", "turn left at the bank".

title: A new neighbour
lines: Hello! Are you my new neighbour?
Yes, I am. My name is Leo. I'm new here.
Nice to meet you, Leo. I'm Helen. I live next door.
Nice to meet you too. Is this a quiet street?
Yes, very quiet. Where are you from?
I'm from Spain, but I work here in Leeds now.
Welcome to Leeds! Do you live alone?
No, I live with my wife and our little dog.
A little dog? Is it white?
Yes, she is. Her name is Coco. Why?
Because there is a small white dog in my garden right now!
Oh no! I'm so sorry. She loves gardens.
Don't worry. I love dogs. Come in and have a cup of tea.
Thank you, Helen. That's very kind of you.

gloss.neighbour: a person who lives near you
gloss.meet: see and talk to someone for the first time
gloss.next: next door: in the house beside this one
gloss.street: a road in a town, with houses
gloss.welcome: we are happy that you are here
gloss.wife: the woman a man is married to
gloss.garden: the land by a house, with grass and flowers
gloss.sorry: a word you say when you feel bad about something
gloss.worry: don't worry: it is all right
gloss.cup: a small thing you drink from
gloss.kind: good and friendly to other people

questions.q: Which country is Leo from?
Where is the little dog right now?

notice: A short answer repeats only the first verb, not the whole sentence: "Yes, I am", "Yes, she is".

title: At the pharmacy
lines: Hello. How can I help you?
Hi. I've had a sore throat and a bad cough for three days.
I see. Do you have a temperature?
No, I don't think so. But I can't sleep because of the cough.
Are you taking any other medicine at the moment?
No, nothing. Could I have some antibiotics, please?
I'm sorry, I can't sell antibiotics without a prescription from a doctor.
Oh, I didn't know that. What can I take instead?
This cough syrup is very good. Take two spoonfuls before bed. And these tablets will help your throat.
How often should I take the tablets?
One every four hours, but not more than six a day.
All right, I'll take both. How much is that?
That's eighteen dollars. If you don't feel better in three days, you should see a doctor.
I will. Thank you for your help.

gloss.throat: the inside of your neck, where food goes down
gloss.cough: a sudden loud noise in your throat when you are ill
gloss.temperature: have a temperature: your body is hotter than normal
gloss.medicine: something you take to get better
gloss.antibiotics: a strong medicine that only a doctor can give you
gloss.prescription: a doctor's paper that says which medicine you can buy
gloss.should: it is a good idea to

questions.q: Why can the customer not sleep?
What does the customer need to buy antibiotics?

notice: Should asks for advice and gives it: "How often should I take the tablets?", "you should see a doctor".

title: Checking in at a hotel
lines: Good evening, and welcome. Do you have a reservation?
Good evening. Yes, I booked a room for three nights. The name is Elena Rossi.
Let me check. Yes, here it is. A double room on the second floor.
A double room? But I booked a room with two single beds. I'm travelling with my brother.
Oh, I'm very sorry. There is a mistake in our system.
Can you change it, please? We really need two beds.
I'm afraid we have no twin rooms tonight. But I can give you a bigger room with a sofa bed.
Is it more expensive?
No, it's the same price.
And is the sofa bed comfortable?
Yes, very comfortable. And tomorrow I can move you to a twin room.
All right, that sounds fine. What time is breakfast?
Breakfast is from seven to ten in the dining room. Here is your key. The lift is on your left.
Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome. Enjoy your stay!

gloss.reservation: a room that the hotel keeps for you
gloss.check: look to see if it is right
gloss.double: double room: a room with one big bed
gloss.system: the computer program that the hotel uses
gloss.afraid: I'm afraid: I am sorry to say
gloss.twin: twin room: a room with two single beds
gloss.sofa: sofa bed: a seat that opens to make a bed
gloss.comfortable: nice to sit or sleep on
gloss.sounds: that sounds fine: I think that is good
gloss.dining: dining room: the room where people eat
gloss.key: the thing that opens a door
gloss.lift: a machine that carries people up and down
gloss.stay: the time you spend in the hotel

questions.q: Who is the guest travelling with?
What kind of bed is in the bigger room?

notice: Can is used both to ask for help and to offer it: "Can you change it, please?", "I can give you a bigger room".

title: Booking a table
lines: Good afternoon, the Old Mill restaurant. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a table for Saturday evening, please.
Certainly. For how many people?
For six people, at eight o'clock if possible.
I'm sorry, we're full at eight. I have a table at half past six or at nine.
Nine is too late for the children. Half past six is better.
No problem. Would you like to sit inside, or outside in the garden?
In the garden, please, if the weather is good.
Of course. Can I have your name, please?
It's Marco Costa. And I have one more question.
Yes, of course. Go ahead.
It's my mother's birthday. Can we bring our own cake?
Certainly. We can keep it in the kitchen and bring it out with candles.
That would be perfect. Thank you very much.
You're welcome. See you on Saturday at half past six.
See you then. Goodbye!

gloss.book: ask a restaurant to keep a table for you
gloss.possible: if possible: if you can do it
gloss.half: half past six: thirty minutes after six
gloss.outside: not in the building, in the open air
gloss.garden: a place with grass and plants beside a building
gloss.weather: sun, rain, wind, hot or cold
gloss.question: something you ask
gloss.birthday: the day of the year when a person was born
gloss.own: our own: one that is ours
gloss.candles: small sticks that burn with a light, for a birthday cake (candle)
gloss.perfect: as good as it can be
gloss.then: see you then: see you at that time

questions.q: Where does the customer want to sit?
Whose birthday is it on Saturday?

notice: Would like is a polite way to say want. Use it to ask and to answer: "I'd like to book a table", "Would you like to sit inside".

title: Returning faulty headphones
lines: Hi there. How can I help you today?
Hello. I bought these headphones here two weeks ago, and the left side has stopped working.
Oh dear. Have you tried charging them fully?
Yes, I've tried everything in the instructions, but nothing makes any difference.
I see. Do you have your receipt with you?
Yes, here it is. I paid by card, if that helps.
Thank you. Well, we could send them away to be repaired, but that usually takes about three weeks.
I'd rather not wait that long. Could I exchange them for a new pair instead?
Let me check. I'm afraid we've sold out of the black ones. We only have them in white at the moment.
In that case, I'd prefer to have my money back, if that's possible.
Of course. Since they're faulty, you're entitled to a full refund. It'll go back onto your card within five days.
That's fine. Do I need to sign anything?
Just here, please. And I'm sorry about the trouble.
No problem at all. Thanks for sorting it out so quickly.

gloss.headphones: things you wear on your ears to listen to music
gloss.tried: done to see if it works (try)
gloss.instructions: the paper that tells you how to use something
gloss.receipt: the paper that shows what you paid
gloss.rather: I'd rather not: I would prefer not to
gloss.exchange: give back and take another one
gloss.afraid: I'm afraid: I am sorry to say
gloss.sold: sold out of: have none left to sell (sell)
gloss.case: in that case: if that is so
gloss.entitled: entitled to: having the right to get
gloss.refund: money given back to a customer
gloss.sign: write your name on a paper
gloss.sorting: sorting it out: solving the problem (sort out)

questions.q: Which side of the headphones has stopped working?
What does the customer ask for in the end?

notice: I'd rather (not) + verb and I'd prefer to + verb say politely what you want: "I'd rather not wait that long", "I'd prefer to have my money back".

title: Viewing a flat
lines: Come in. This is the living room. It gets the sun all afternoon.
It's brighter than I expected. Is the furniture included?
Yes, everything you can see stays, including the washing machine in the kitchen.
That's good to know. And how much is the rent exactly?
Nine hundred pounds a month, plus a deposit of one month's rent.
Does that include any bills, or are they extra?
Water is included. Gas, electricity and internet are separate.
I see. How is the flat heated? It feels a bit cold in here.
There are radiators in every room. To be honest, the boiler is rather old, but the landlord has promised to replace it before winter.
Could that promise be written into the contract?
I can certainly ask him. Is there anything else you'd like to know?
Yes. When would the flat be available, and how long is the contract?
From the first of next month, for at least twelve months.
It's the nicest flat I've seen so far, but I need a day to think it over.
Of course. Just let me know by Friday, because two other people are viewing it tomorrow.
I'll call you tomorrow afternoon. Thanks for showing me around.

gloss.furniture: tables, chairs, beds and other large things in a home
gloss.included: part of what you get for the price (include)
gloss.rent: the money you pay every month for a home
gloss.exactly: with no mistake, the true number
gloss.deposit: money paid at the start and given back at the end
gloss.bills: what you pay for water, gas and electricity (bill)
gloss.extra: added on top of the price
gloss.electricity: the power for lights and machines
gloss.separate: not together, paid for on their own
gloss.radiators: metal heaters on the wall, with hot water inside (radiator)
gloss.honest: to be honest: to tell the truth
gloss.boiler: the machine that heats the water for a home
gloss.landlord: the person who owns the home you pay to live in
gloss.promised: said that he would surely do it (promise)
gloss.replace: put a new one in its place
gloss.promise: something you say you will surely do
gloss.contract: the paper with the rules that both people sign
gloss.over: think it over: think carefully before deciding
gloss.showing: showing me around: taking me through the rooms (show around)

questions.q: Which bill is included in the rent?
What has the landlord promised to replace?

notice: The passive (be + past participle) puts the thing first when it matters more than who acts: "Is the furniture included?", "How is the flat heated?"
